headlines.article_text: Trump administration moves to cut food stamps for 6.3 million people Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu A resident browses donated food items in the pantry at Feeding South Florida in Pembroke Park, Florida, US, on Friday, Oct. 31, 2025. About 42 million Americans could see their food assistance cut off within days as the US government shutdown stretches toward its second month, threatening to deepen economic pain and test Washington's resolve in one of the longest funding lapses in US history. Photographer: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images Eva Marie Uzcategui | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Trump administration on Tuesday moved to cut millions more Americans from the nation's largest food assistance program, even as enrollment continues to fall from other administration cuts. A proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture would curb automatic eligibility for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, for households receiving cash aid under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families Program. Currently, households receiving TANF benefits qualify for SNAP without needing to meet federal income thresholds. TANF eligibility varies by state but is generally 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level. SNAP eligibility is generally 130% of the federal poverty level. Under the USDA's proposed change, nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits, according to an agency analysis included in the proposed rule. The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and "preserve benefits for the truly needy," the rule said. More than 5.5 million people have already lost SNAP benefits since President Donald Trump enacted cuts to the program in his July 2025 tax law, bringing enrollment to about 36 million people, according to USDA data. The enrollment decline is partly due to struggles by states to implement administrative changes to the program and also to absorb significant new costs from Trump's law. Because SNAP enrollment also confers eligibility for other food aid programs, the USDA estimates that 1.8 million children would also lose eligibility for free school lunch under its proposed rule. Democratic Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota, ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, in a statement called the rule "heartless and cruel." "The proposed rule would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs," she said. The public will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule. David Ryder | Reuters Boeing said on Tuesday it delivered 49 jets in October, down from 57 the previous month and 53 a year earlier. However, Boeing had its strongest October for orders minus cancellations since 1997, booking 165 new orders with no cancellations. Most of those came from lessor Avolon's order for 140 737 MAX jets. Boeing delivered 32 737 MAX jets in October, down from 43 in September, with CEO Kelly Ortberg saying last month that it would miss its 737 delivery target of about 500 jets this year. Deliveries also included 11 787 Dreamliners, two 777 freighters and three 767s, including one for Boeing Defense's KC-46 tanker program. The lower deliveries come as Boeing works to raise 737 production to 47 jets a month, a rate Ortberg said the company would reach in early 2027. Wing production for 737 jets remains a constraint, and a supplier dispute has stalled wing production for 777 freighters and 767s. Through October, the US planemaker has delivered 524 jets, up about 6% from 493 a year earlier, well behind European rival Airbus , which delivered 621 in the first 10 months of the year. Air New Zealand took delivery of two 787s despite still waiting for certification by European regulators of its economy-class Skyrest sleep pods, according to the airline and news reports. Of the October orders, 150 were for 737 MAX jets: 140 for Avolon, six for Allegiant Air and four for unidentified customers. The other 15 were 787s for unidentified customers. headlines.title: Ex-Google recruiter: You're answering 'Tell me about yourself?' all wrong, and other job interview mistakes—do this instead
headlines.summary: Former Google recruiter Farah Sharghi shares her best advice for how to turn coffee chats into real introductions and interviews.
headlines.article_text: Ex-Google recruiter how to avoid 3 common job interview mistakes Skip Navigation Related Stories Work Ex-Google recruiter: Why this common mistake makes your resume 'invisible' Work 3 signs work is consuming your life—and what to do about it: ‘Catch it now,' says expert Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Psychology and Relationships 5 ways to be more yourself and stop worrying if you're ‘good enough’ Raising Successful Kids I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on Solstock | E+ | Getty Images In a job market that can seem impossible to break into, relationships still matter and are often what will get your foot in the door. But if your coffee chats and informational interviews keep ending with "Let's stay in touch," and then nothing happens, you might be wondering where you went wrong. I've spent more than a decade recruiting for companies like Google, TikTok, Uber and The New York Times. I've found that when people try to network, one of the biggest things that trips them up is the seemingly simple question: "Tell me about yourself?" It can unlock referrals, more introductions and interviews — but only if you know how to answer it. When someone recommends you for a role at their company, they are often asked to fill out a form where they write how they know you and why you'd be good at the job. That note is where your coffee chat either turns into an interview or goes nowhere. So the next time you are meeting with someone who does the work you want to do, or is employed at your dream company, remember that you're not there to impress them. You want to help them answer the question they will be asked afterward, which is "Why should we talk to this person?" Here's my best advice for how to navigate three of the most common job interview mistakes. Answer 'Tell me about yourself?' in 30 words or less When they hear "So, tell me about yourself," most people answer with a list of their accomplishments. The problem with that is that it gives your potential referrer nothing to hold on to. That's the wrong approach. Instead, break down the answer into three parts. Who are you now? One simple line. "I'm a supply chain analyst." What is the career move you're trying to make? Be specific. "Interested in moving into strategy" tells them something about your actionable goals. "Looking for growth" is vague and doesn't give them anything to work with. Why did you reach out to them? You wanted to talk to this person for a reason. Cogently explain why. They likely made the career move you want, or they're in the role you're aiming for. This is how it should sound when you combine them: "I'm a supply chain analyst. I reached out because you moved from operations into strategy and that's exactly what I would like to do." That's under 30 words and it gives your informational interviewer a clear place to start when they recommend you. "Supply chain analyst moving from operations into strategy" is the first line of your referral note, and you just wrote it for them. You want to avoid this this 'typical' question You've cleared that first hurdle, but the next mistake people often make is that they will ask: "What is a typical day for you?" This will only get you a vague, unhelpful description of their responsibilities. A stronger question is: "What part of your job do you find to be the most rewarding?" When you ask this, they have to think about a specific moment, instead of a general list. This way you will find out what the job feels like on a good day, which the job description will never tell you. Follow that up with "How is your performance measured at the end of the year?" When a hiring manager opens a new role, in my experience, one of the first things the recruiter asks them is, "What does success look like in the first 30 days and in the first 90 days?" But almost none of that makes it into the job description either. With this approach, you get specific and quantified details that will help you better frame your expertise in an interview setting. Invite your conversation partner to tell you a story You're almost there, but now another trap is waiting for you. You're talking with someone you admire and whose expertise you value, so an understandable question is: "What advice would you give to someone who is just starting out?" Please don't do this. It will generally only yield a response like "work hard" or "be curious." To get the information that will actually help you in the next phase of your job hunt, ask these questions instead: "When you think about a recent new hire you enjoyed working with, what qualities come to mind?" When you ask about one person who did well, that means they have to give you specifics. Then with those details, you can share a related anecdote about how you have demonstrated those traits in your previous work. "What has surprised you most about your role?" You can also ask "What do you wish you'd known before you took the job?" Surprise doesn't necessarily connote a negative experience, but this question is a great way to subtly find out where the pitfalls and unexpected stressors are. Even if you are trying to suss out what someone doesn't like about their job, phrasing it this way won't set off any alarm bells for people who won't ever complain about their employer. "What's happening in the industry right now that you think more people should know about?" You hear their view, you get to share yours and demonstrate that you've done your homework. And you can use what they tell you in your next real interview. Before your meeting ends, make sure to ask "Based on what we discussed today, is there anyone else you think I should talk to?" It's important to highlight the discussion part first. Without it, you're asking them to go through everyone they know and pick someone at random. They'll probably say "Let me think about it." But with the first part, you've narrowed it down for them. The worst they can say is "Sorry, I can't think of anyone," and that's fine. But ask every time.
